name: Tara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In the week I'm a renovation carpenter for Whitcombe Builders, mostly kitchens, staircases and knocking old houses about for families who've just moved in. Right now it's a Victorian terrace on Hazel Road where we're putting in a new staircase and opening up the back room. At weekends I build garden sheds and summerhouses under my own name, Tanaka Timber, out of my garage. I love making something from a pile of planks, and I hate customers who change their minds after the wood's cut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the weekend business work, day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The AI does half my office work. A customer sends me a photo of their garden, I ask the AI to sketch three shed designs with prices, and I send them back the same evening. It writes my posts for the local groups and helps with my accounts, I use it every single day. My husband Graham, he was in the army and now does security at the hospital, says I'm running a little empire from the garage, but it's maybe twenty sheds a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Well, it's not hype in my garage, but I take your point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a brilliant tool for small businesses, and people should stop expecting miracles from it. I'd probably post a little video of how I do a shed quote in ten minutes. Somebody's grandmother will love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, that suits me. I keep my edge over the old-school shed builders who still draw on the back of an envelope, and nobody loses their job. I'd keep working at Whitcombe and keep growing the sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep both going. Whitcombe for the steady wage, sheds at weekends, maybe push it to thirty sheds a year. I'd put the shed profits into savings, we've got about four months put by, and maybe buy a better mitre saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan for retirement in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop at Whitcombe at sixty-two or sixty-three and do sheds part-time until my back says no. Graham's got his army pension, so we'd be comfortable enough. I'd never fully stop, I'd go mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do any of the lads at Whitcombe use the AI like you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only Kemal, and he's thirty. The others think I'm showing off. Then they ask me to sort their holiday bookings on it.

S0.say: It's a brilliant tool for small businesses, so people should stop expecting miracles from it. I'd probably post a video of how I quote a shed in ten minutes.
S0.think: That suits me, because I keep my edge over shed builders who draw on the back of an envelope and nobody loses their job. I'd keep Whitcombe and grow the sheds.
S0.do: Keeps her Whitcombe job and grows the weekend shed business towards thirty sheds a year. Puts profits into savings and buys a better mitre saw.
S0.quote: The others think I'm showing off. Then they ask me to sort their holiday bookings on it.
S0.fieldNote: She already runs a small side business powered by daily AI use. A plateau suits her because she keeps her edge. Her husband's army pension provides some security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, but people still working. That's the one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on with it, the ones who learn will do well and the ones who moan won't. That's how it's always been, from the plough to the power drill. And I'd say government should stay out of the way and let small firms get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm already quicker on quotes than anyone round here. If there's a cheap machine that cuts shed parts from a design, I'd want one in the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at cutting machines this year, the ones that cut parts from a computer design, and see if the bank would lend me a few thousand. I'd push the shed business towards a proper second income, and talk to Graham about whether I could drop to four days at Whitcombe. I'd keep using the AI for everything office-side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited. A bit like when I bought my first van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd borrow money at fifty-eight. Is that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, I won't pretend. But it'd be a few thousand, not a fortune, and the machine would pay for itself in maybe fifteen sheds. Graham would want to see the sums written down, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham, maybe. Security is cameras now, and the cameras are getting cleverer. But he's sixty-one and has his army pension, so he'd be all right even if they cut his hours.

S1.say: Get on with it: the ones who learn will do well and the ones who moan won't, same as from the plough to the power drill. Government should stay out of the way and let small firms get on with it.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because I'm already quicker on quotes than anyone round here. If there's a cheap machine that cuts shed parts from a design, I want one in the garage.
S1.do: Researches computer-controlled cutting machines this year and asks the bank to lend a few thousand. Grows the shed business into a proper second income and discusses dropping to four days at Whitcombe.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like buying her first van.
S1.quote: That's how it's always been, from the plough to the power drill.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as a chance to invest and automate her own small business. She's honest about the risk of borrowing and defers to her husband's caution on the sums. Her free-market view includes wanting government out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Full AGI and robots doing the building. Goodness. That changes the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always, but I'd be less cheerful saying it. And I'd say this is a chance for people who own their own tools to do well, if they move fast. I'd post about it, but I wouldn't pretend it was easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years the big factories would be churning out sheds with robots cheaper than I could ever do. My edge would be gone, and Whitcombe would buy robots for kitchens soon after. I'd be sixty, with four months saved and a loan on a cutting machine if I'd bought one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't borrow for the machine, not on two years' notice. I'd squeeze as many sheds as I could out of the next two years while people still want a person, and bank every penny. I'd look at whether I could sell custom work the factories won't touch, odd-shaped gardens, matching old windows, and I'd use the AI to find those customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not beaten, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for work the factories won't touch. Is there really any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. There's always someone with a sloping garden and a Victorian house who wants it to look right. But if the robots can do anything a person can, then that's only a while, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Graham that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, pour us a drink, we need to talk about the sheds. He'd say I'm getting ahead of myself. Then he'd get the calculator out, because that's what we do.

S2.say: Adapt or get left behind, same as always, though I'd be less cheerful saying it. People who own their own tools could do well if they move fast, but I wouldn't pretend it was easy.
S2.think: In two years the factories would turn out robot-built sheds cheaper than I ever could, and Whitcombe would buy robots too. I'd be sixty with four months saved.
S2.do: Holds off borrowing for a cutting machine and builds as many sheds as possible while people still want a person, banking every penny. Uses AI to find customers for custom work the factories won't do.
S2.quote: If the robots can do anything a person can, then that's only a while, and I know that.
S2.fieldNote: Two years flips her from investing to protecting cash, a sensible change for a risk-taker. She's clear-eyed that her custom niche only buys time. Her belief in markets holds, but she admits it cuts against her this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for anyone willing to work to get ahead of this. Small businesses should be buying the machines, not just the big firms. And I'd say families should be talking about it at the kitchen table, not waiting for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is enough to make money from it before it takes over. I'd buy the cutting machine, and maybe one of the first small building robots when they're affordable, and run Tanaka Timber with fewer hands. By sixty-three I'd sell the business or hand it on and stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd buy the cutting machine, borrowing a bit, and drop to four days at Whitcombe. I'd spend evenings learning whatever software runs the robots, with the AI teaching me. I'd ask my son Daniel if he wants in, because a family business is worth more than a garage hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you want Daniel involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He runs a little gym and works too many hours for too little money. If the sheds became a proper business with machines, it could be his when I stop. That's how my dad did it with his garage, and it's the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the machine to pay for itself before the price of everything drops. In two years I'd be scared to borrow. In five, I'd borrow, use it, earn it back and sell up while the business is still worth something.

S3.say: There's time for anyone willing to work to get ahead of this. Small businesses should be buying the machines too, and families should talk it over at the kitchen table instead of waiting for the government.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make money from it before it takes over. I'd run Tanaka Timber with machines and fewer hands, then sell or hand it on at sixty-three.
S3.do: Buys a cutting machine next year with a small loan and drops to four days at Whitcombe. Learns robot software in the evenings with AI's help and invites her son into the business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, like a race she thinks she can run.
S3.quote: A family business is worth more than a garage hobby.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she returns to investing and automating, timing an exit before prices collapse. Family succession, modelled on her father's garage, is part of her plan. She is clear about why two years would make her too scared to borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. Oh, I could do a lot with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance in a generation for people who are willing to work hard and learn. Set something up, buy the machines, own a piece of it. I'd say that to every young person I met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one's good for me. I'd build Tanaka Timber up properly with machines over five or six years, hand it to Daniel, and retire comfortably. If it all goes robotic in 2036, at least our family owns some of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first couple of years, I'd buy the cutting machine, rent a small unit instead of the garage, and maybe leave Whitcombe at sixty to run the sheds full time. I'd use the AI for design and marketing every day. And I'd get Daniel trained up alongside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. More than calm, excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very positive. Is there anything about it that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy, my daughter, she's a primary teacher, and I don't know what happens to schools in all this. And I'd worry about people who aren't like me, who don't want to start a business. Not everyone's built for it, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should happen for those people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their families and communities should help them first, that's what families are for. And the government should help people train or start something, not just pay them to stay home. Work gives people a reason to get up.

S4.say: This is the best chance in a generation for people willing to work hard and learn. Set something up, buy the machines and own a piece of it.
S4.think: This one's good for me: I'd build Tanaka Timber up with machines, hand it to Daniel and retire comfortably. If it all goes robotic in 2036, at least our family owns some of the robots.
S4.do: Buys a cutting machine and rents a small unit within two years, possibly leaving Whitcombe at sixty to run the sheds full time. Trains her son alongside her and uses AI daily for design and marketing.
S4.feel: Calm, and more than that, excited.
S4.quote: If it all goes robotic in 2036, at least our family owns some of the robots.
S4.fieldNote: The decade turns this into an opportunity she clearly relishes. She recognises not everyone is built for business, and prefers family and community support plus help to train over income support. Her worry for her teacher daughter is genuine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where I can't get ahead of it. I'd be scared to borrow, the factories would beat me on price, and I'd be sixty. What would help is a bit of time, honestly, and maybe tax breaks or cheap loans for small firms to buy the machines, so it's not only the big companies who own them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people whether they want to own the machines or just work next to them. Most people never think about it. I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.
portrait: Tara Tanaka is a 58-year-old renovation carpenter at Whitcombe Builders who also runs a weekend shed business, Tanaka Timber, from her garage, using AI every day for designs, quotes and posts. She's calm and keen in the first two pictures and would borrow to buy a cutting machine. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, because factories would beat her on price before she could adapt, so she'd stop borrowing and bank cash. With five or ten years she'd invest, automate and bring her son into the business. She believes in markets and family, and would rather own the robot than be replaced by it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the only picture where she can't get ahead: she'd be scared to borrow, factories would undercut her, and she'd be sixty.
whatWouldHelp: More time, and tax breaks or cheap loans so small firms can buy the machines too, not just big companies.
